original comment (summary): Novelty limited: the framework combines established techniques (SD v1.5, LoRA, DCT embedding, LSB, Huffman, CRC, adaptive selection); the DCT reward is not shown to be a substantial advance over frequency-aware generative steganography; a clearer technical distinction is needed.
what the revised manuscript does: Introduction states the embedder is assembled from standard components and serves as a test bed; contributions are restated as a reward-guided fine-tuning objective plus a controlled evaluation; diffusion is used only as the cover source, unlike methods that embed in the diffusion process (CRoSS, GSD/StegoDiffusion, PSyDUCK, Stable Diffusion latent methods); reward fine-tuning precedent (DDPO, DRaFT) is cited.
evidence: Text in main.tex; no experiment against frequency-aware generative methods
remaining work: The distinction is argued in text only. No same-data experiment against a frequency-aware generative scheme (they solve a different problem: lossy-channel recovery).
response to reviewer: We agree that the components are established. We now state this explicitly and restrict the contribution to a reward-guided fine-tuning objective for cover generation and a controlled measurement of what it changes; we explain why diffusion-as-channel methods are not directly comparable.

original comment (summary): Steganalysis shows a security weakness: near-random accuracy at the native SRNet threshold is threshold miscalibration; calibrated accuracy 71.8 to 82.7%, AUC up to 0.836; security claims unsupported.
what the revised manuscript does: All security claims withdrawn (Introduction scope paragraph, Discussion). The old detector is replaced by (a) an SRNet-style CNN trained from scratch on a universal DCT embedding with its threshold fixed on its own validation set, and (b) SPAM detectors trained on DEDS with subject-grouped CV. Threshold-free AUC and P_E reported; matched detectors reach AUC 1.000; text states the trained-threshold result does not show indistinguishability.
evidence: claim_ledger.csv C22 to C31; universal_dct_steganalysis_results.xlsx; steganalysis_spam.csv
remaining work: None.
response to reviewer: We agree. All security claims are removed. We report threshold-free AUC and P_E, and detectors trained on our embedder detect it almost perfectly (AUC 1.000).

original comment (summary): Comparison not rigorous or fair: results from different studies compared directly; J-UNIWARD, S-UNIWARD, WOW and J-MiPOD not evaluated on the same cover/stego data with the same steganalyser.
what the revised manuscript does: Cross-paper numeric comparison removed (Discussion states no ranking is implied). S-UNIWARD, WOW and LSB matching run on the same 1,000 pairs, same luminance planes, same number of payload bits per image, same SPAM detector protocol (entropy-bound simulation). J-UNIWARD and J-MiPOD not run; justified because the stego object is a losslessly stored spatial image.
location: Results, Detectability; Table 3; Methods, Reference embedders; Discussion, limitations
evidence: steganalysis_spam.csv; analysis1000/steganalysis_wow.csv; wow.py verified against brute force (relative error 1e-13)
remaining work: Spatial baselines: done (simulated at the entropy bound, not STC-coded; baselines were not scored by the CNN). JPEG-domain baselines: not run. A reviewer may argue DEDS also requantises luminance with a JPEG-like table; a contextual J-UNIWARD run on JPEG versions of the covers at matched bits would close this.
response to reviewer: S-UNIWARD, WOW and LSB matching were run on the same covers, payloads and detector; both adaptive schemes are markedly less detectable than DEDS. J-UNIWARD and J-MiPOD embed in JPEG files, whereas our stego object is a lossless spatial image, so no like-for-like comparison exists; we state this as a limitation.

original comment (summary): Extremely poor robustness: 0% full recovery under JPEG 90, resizing, noise, blur, cropping, geometric changes; Hamming(7,4) fails; method restricted to a clean lossless channel.
what the revised manuscript does: No robustness claim; scope restricted to lossless storage (Abstract, Introduction, Discussion). Table 4 on 1,000 covers; Supplementary Table S1 includes the Hamming(7,4) simulation; new repeated-message test (Supplementary Table S6) shows recovery only after own-table requantisation or at about 27 bytes.
location: Abstract; Results, Message recovery after lossy processing; Table 4; Supp. Tables S1, S6; Discussion
remaining work: The weakness is inherent to the embedder and is not fixed; it is measured and stated. Additional measurements were added.
response to reviewer: We agree. The paper now claims exact recovery on a lossless channel only, reports the failures in full, and adds a repeated-message test that shows the limits of redundancy.

original comment (summary): Figures look stylised/generic, have small unclear text, and do not expose operations, data flow or module interactions; redesign as technically informative, editable diagrams.
what the revised manuscript does: Fig. 1 redrawn as a vector schematic with equations, tensor shapes and gradient path (script fig_schematic.py, editable); Figs. 2 to 4 are data plots generated from the result files.

original comment (summary): Practical benefit of the costly diffusion stage not established; no comprehensive computational complexity/runtime comparison; trade-off not compelling given detectability and fragility.
what the revised manuscript does: Computational cost section: generation 1.9/3.0 s, DEDS embedding 15 to 85 s, extraction 0.12 s, fine-tuning 18 to 24 h (authors' records), and measured S-UNIWARD/WOW cost computation 0.12 s per image on the same processor; Discussion states DEDS is far more expensive and that its benefit is limited to capacity and to one detector.
location: Results, Computational cost; Supp. Table S4; Discussion
evidence: embed_rerun.csv; timing measured 11 Oct 2026 (20 covers, single process)
remaining work: Fine-tuning time comes from the authors' records, not a log.
response to reviewer: We now report measured runtimes for every stage and for S-UNIWARD and WOW on the same processor, and we state plainly that DEDS is far more expensive.

original comment (summary): Use a well-established detector (maxSRM with fast linear classifier), less sensitive to cover-source mismatch; CSM literature not reported.
what the revised manuscript does: CSM literature cited (Giboulot et al. 2020) to explain why detectors trained on photographs fail. SPAM (686) with shrinkage LDA used instead of maxSRM; Discussion states rich-model features would give tighter estimates.
remaining work: maxSRM not run. Minimum work: SRM/maxSRM feature extraction (e.g. a Python port such as the one in the Aletheia toolbox) on 2,000 to 4,000 images and an FLD ensemble with the same subject-grouped CV; roughly 3 to 5 hours.
response to reviewer: We cite the CSM literature and use detectors trained on the same source. We did not run maxSRM; a simple SPAM detector already detects DEDS with AUC 1.000, so a stronger detector cannot change that conclusion.
